conflicts.topic: Identifier and type of the 2025 generative AI standard

side_a.says: Header prints 'PSG Number: PS-25-001'; Purpose says 'This policy establishes'.

side_b.section: GS-25-001 Related Enterprise PSGs, p.12; GS-25-002 Related Enterprise PSGs, p.6; SS-25-001 Standard section, p.2
side_b.says: Sibling documents cite it as 'Generative AI Responsible Use SS-25-001'; its own body is headed 'STANDARD' and says 'State government employees shall follow this standard'.

conflicts.note: The corpus does not settle which identifier or document type is correct.

side_a.section: Related Enterprise Policies, Standards, and Guidelines, p.3

side_b.says: The attached standard titled 'Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use' is numbered SS-23-002; no SS-23-001 is attached.

conflicts.note: Either a typographical error or a reference to a document outside the attached set; also recorded as an unresolved reference.

side_a.says: 'tools or systems used to create models that can generate new and original content, such as images, music, or text, based on patterns and examples from existing data.'

side_b.section: SS-23-002 Terms and Definitions, p.2; SS-25-001 Terms and Definitions, p.1
side_b.says: 'a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.' Both standards give the PS-23-001 wording as the definition of 'Generative AI'.

conflicts.note: Under PS-23-001's wording the policy's procurement-review rule would cover only content-generating tools; under the standards' wording 'AI' is broader.

conflicts.topic: Entering personal, sensitive or regulated data into a GenAI tool: whether an exception exists and who can approve it

side_a.says: PII, PHI or other regulated data 'shall not be used as inputs to GenAI tools unless formally approved by the GTA’s Office of Artificial Intelligence.'

side_b.section: SS-23-002 6(a), p.9; GS-25-001 Use AI Tools Safely and Properly, p.2; Strategies for Data Privacy and AI, p.4; Rubric, p.10; SS-25-001 3.0 table (Data analysis & reports), p.7
side_b.says: SS-23-002: confidential, sensitive and personal data 'must be authorized by appropriate agency authority'. GS-25-001: 'do not provide them with confidential or private state information, or personal records' and 'Do not enter personal and/or sensitive data into a GenAI model' (no exception stated); elsewhere consult 'their department's data privacy officer or designated compliance authority' and avoid input 'without approval'; Rubric allows it only with 'explicit approval from the Georgia Technology Authority'. SS-25-001 table: 'Don’t use GenAI to analyze or process personally identifiable or regulated data' (no exception stated).

conflicts.note: Three different approvers (GTA Office of AI; appropriate agency authority; GTA generally) and two flat prohibitions. The data categories also differ in wording across the documents and none is defined.

conflicts.topic: Personal email / personal accounts for GenAI tools

side_a.says: 'The use of personal email addresses for such access is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the agency’s technology leadership.'

side_b.section: Use AI Tools Safely and Properly, p.2
side_b.says: 'avoid using personal accounts, such as personal email addresses, within any software' (no exception; phrased as advice).

conflicts.note: Different strength (prohibited vs avoid) and only the standard provides an exception.

conflicts.topic: When AI assistance has to be labeled or cited

side_a.says: 'Any content generated or assisted by GenAI shall be clearly labeled'.

side_b.section: How to Properly Cite AI-Generated Content, p.9; Use AI Tools Safely and Properly, pp.2-3; Do Not Put Private Data at Risk, p.4
side_b.says: 'if the AI model helps a user in generating their own content and ideas, citation isn’t necessary'. The same guideline also says 'Anything produced with the assistance of AI should be cited correctly', 'Cite and acknowledge all AI-generated, brainstormed, or edited content', and 'All AI-generated content ... must be clearly labeled as AI-generated'.

conflicts.note: SS-25-001 covers content merely 'assisted' by GenAI. GS-25-001 exempts tool-like assistance in one section and asks for brainstormed and edited content to be cited in another, so the guideline also conflicts with itself.

conflicts.topic: What an attribution / citation has to contain

side_a.says: Standardized attribution formats 'that include': name of the GenAI tool used; summary of the prompt or task; identity of the staff who reviewed or edited the content.

side_b.section: How to Properly Cite AI-Generated Content, pp.9-10
side_b.says: Informal documents: acknowledge that AI was used and which AI model. More official documents: name of the AI model, the name of the prompt used, the company to which the AI model belongs, and the date the content was generated.

conflicts.note: The standard asks for the reviewer's identity, which the guideline does not; the guideline asks for company and date, which the standard does not. SS-25-001's own example omits the prompt summary.

conflicts.topic: Pre-procurement review of AI tools: process and channel

side_a.says: Procurement of GenAI products or services must 'Be approved in advance by the Georgia Technology Authority (GTA) by completing the review form at https://ai.georgia.gov/ai-application-and-tool-request-form'; agencies must consult the GTA Office of Artificial Intelligence before contracting.

side_b.says: SS-23-002: 'Agencies shall submit a Business Solutions Review (BSR) Request form to GTA via email, gta.psg@gta.ga.gov ... prior to procurement'. PS-23-001: agencies 'shall submit all software, applications, tools, and services utilizing AI for business operations to GTA for review prior to procurement' (no channel named).

conflicts.note: Two different forms and channels. The documents do not say whether the 2025 form replaces the BSR for GenAI or both are needed.

conflicts.topic: Reporting AI tools in use to GTA

side_a.says: Agencies 'shall maintain and report via the agency’s annual STARR report, a current inventory of GenAI systems and applications used or planned'.

side_b.says: Agencies shall 'Report all tools using AI components to GTA via email at gta.psg@gta.ga.gov'.

conflicts.note: Different channel and cadence (annual report vs email with no cadence); scope differs (GenAI systems vs all tools using AI components).

conflicts.topic: Reporting incidents, breaches and misuse: recipient and deadline

side_a.says: 'Agencies shall report significant incidents involving GenAI to the GTA Office of AI within 48 hours.'

side_b.says: Data breaches or incidents involving AI systems go to 'the designated Data Protection Officer (DPO) or other appropriate person(s)'; suspected misuse goes 'to the agency CIO or senior executive and GTA OIS'; risks or ethical concerns in AI development go to 'the agency’s designated Ethics Officer, CIO, and State CIO'. No deadline is stated.

conflicts.note: Different recipients; only the 2025 standard sets a deadline. 'Significant incidents' is not defined, so overlap with the 2023 categories cannot be determined from the text.

conflicts.topic: Modal strength of the 'Keep Human Involvement at the Center' principles

side_a.says: 'State agencies shall establish and adhere to policies'; 'Agencies must maintain clear records'; 'State agencies must ensure that humans retain control'; 'Agencies shall mandate'; 'Agencies must invest in training'; 'State agencies shall retain ownership and control'.

side_b.section: 5GP Keep Human Involvement at the Center, pp.7-9; GS-25-001 Guiding Principles, pp.8-9
side_b.says: The same sentences with 'should': 'State agencies should establish and adhere to policies'; 'Agencies should retain clear records'; 'State agencies should ensure'; 'Agencies should mandate'; 'Agencies should invest'; 'State agencies should retain ownership and control'.

conflicts.note: Same principles, different modal verbs. Principles I-IV also differ in wording and item structure between GS-23-001 and the later text, without a change of modal verb. No document says which wording governs.

conflicts.topic: Keeping versus clearing prompts and responses

side_a.section: Strategies for Data Privacy and AI, p.4
side_a.says: Protecting data 'includes ... minimizing data retention by regularly clearing chats'.

side_b.section: SS-25-001 1.7, p.4; SS-23-002 5(g), p.9; GS-25-001 Use AI Tools Safely and Properly, p.2
side_b.says: SS-25-001: agencies shall 'Retain audit trails of prompts, responses, and reviews'. SS-23-002: 'Maintaining a record of AI tool usage, including the purpose, inputs, outputs, and any actions taken'. GS-25-001: 'Employees should create a record of queries and responses outside of the generative AI software or platform'.

conflicts.note: The texts can be read together (keep the record outside the tool, clear it inside), but none of them says so; left for the reviewer.

conflicts.topic: Who reviews AI-generated content before use

side_a.says: GenAI-generated content 'shall be reviewed and validated by qualified personnel before being used in any official capacity'; Qualified Personnel is 'any subject-matter focused state employee who would otherwise have been responsible for the content in the absence of the AI tool'.

side_b.says: Agencies shall ensure AI-generated content 'is properly reviewed and approved by the business owner or designated personnel before it is published or used for decision-making' and 'Establish a system of checks and balances involving multiple reviewers'.

conflicts.note: Different reviewer (the responsible subject-matter employee vs business owner or designee; one reviewer vs multiple) and different trigger ('any official capacity' vs 'published or used for decision-making').

open_questions.question: Are the 2023 documents (PS-23-001, SS-23-002, GS-23-001) still in force alongside the 2025 documents for generative AI use, and which governs where they differ?
open_questions.why_undecided: No document states that it supersedes, replaces or amends another. SS-25-001, GS-25-001 and GS-25-002 list the 2023 documents as 'related'. Conflicts C04, C08, C09, C10, C11 and C13 turn on this.

open_questions.question: Is 'Generative AI Responsible Use' a policy or a standard, and is its identifier PS-25-001 or SS-25-001?
open_questions.why_undecided: See conflict C01. This inventory uses SS-25-001 and type 'standard' but the choice is not supported by the text alone.

open_questions.question: Do provisions addressed to 'Agencies' or written in the passive voice bind the individual employee?
open_questions.why_undecided: SS-25-001 says 'State government employees shall follow this standard when using commercial GenAI solutions', yet most of its requirements read 'Agencies shall' or name no party (for example 1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.7 and the 3.0 table). SS-23-002 addresses sections 1, 4, 5, 6 and 8 to agencies and section 7 to 'All users of AI systems', while section 11 subjects 'Any state employee' to discipline for violating the standard. The text does not say which agency duties an individual must personally perform. Left for Run 2 and the reviewer.

open_questions.question: Who counts as a 'state employee', 'State government employee' or 'agency personnel', and does the 'Agency' definition limit which employees are covered?
open_questions.why_undecided: None of the terms is defined. The 'Agency' definition excludes the judicial and legislative branches, the Georgia Department of Defense, departments headed by elected constitutional officers, the University System of Georgia and certain authorities; GS-25-001 speaks of 'all state employees' and its header of 'state entities' without that limit. Contractors, temporary staff and interns are not addressed except in SS-23-002 section 11 ('contractor, or vendor').

open_questions.question: What force do 'must', 'shall' and 'is required' carry inside documents labeled guidelines?
open_questions.why_undecided: GS-25-001 says AI-generated content 'must be clearly labeled', photos and videos 'must have a clear watermark', audio 'must include an audio disclaimer', and a citation 'is required'. GS-23-001 principle V uses 'shall' and 'must'. No attached document explains how policies, standards and guidelines differ in binding force (PM-04-001 is cited for that and is not attached). Modal verbs are preserved as written.

open_questions.question: Convention used for provisions that have no modal verb; reviewer to confirm or re-map.
open_questions.why_undecided: The schema allows five modality values. Where the source has no modal verb the wording is preserved in 'modal_as_written' and 'modality' was assigned as follows: positive imperatives in guideline or web-page text ('Opt out of...', 'Require vendors to...') -> should; 'avoid', 'are encouraged', 'is strongly discouraged', 'it is important to', 'it is better to' -> should; 'should not' and 'should never' -> should (no should_not value exists); 'Do not', 'may not', 'is prohibited' and items listed under 'Prohibited' -> must_not; items listed under 'Permissible' or in the 'Acceptable' column -> may; items in the SS-25-001 'Conditional' column -> must; 'is required', 'it is necessary to', 'are responsible for', 'have a duty to', 'is essential' -> must; bullets under a lead-in carry the lead-in's modal. Each of these is a classification choice, not the document's wording.

open_questions.question: May an employee use a free or individually obtained GenAI tool, and are ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot approved?
open_questions.why_undecided: SS-25-001 names those four products only as examples of 'commercial GenAI solutions' and requires GTA approval for 'Any procurement of GenAI products or services'; it does not say whether no-cost sign-up is a procurement. GS-25-001 says employees 'should only use AI which GTA has vetted, with pre-approved vendors' and that approval is version-specific and revocable. No list of vetted tools is attached (UR14).

open_questions.question: Does 'Agencies shall implement additional restrictions based on their specific needs' impose a duty or grant a permission?
open_questions.why_undecided: The sentence uses 'shall' and continues 'but should first consult with' GTA. The preceding sentence speaks of agency 'discretion'. Recorded as written (must). An employee-facing tool would also need each agency's additional restrictions, which are outside the corpus.

open_questions.question: What do the undefined trigger terms mean: 'official capacity', 'moderate-risk use case', 'sensitive data', 'regulated data', 'confidential information', 'state business', 'significant incidents'?
open_questions.why_undecided: Each is a trigger for at least one requirement and none is defined in the attached set (see definitions with status 'used_but_not_defined_in_attached_set'). An AI glossary is cited but not attached (UR23).

open_questions.question: What is the status of the 'Conditional' column in the SS-25-001 use-case table, and when is 'Conditional Approval' needed?
open_questions.why_undecided: The legend reads 'Green = Approved, Yellow = Caution, Red = Prohibited' while the column headings read Acceptable / Conditional / Prohibited. The Conditional cells are written as conditions ('only after review by staff'). The sentence under the table says Conditional Approval 'can be requested' but not for which uses, or whether Conditional-column uses require it. The table is described as examples 'to help agencies interpret and apply this Standard', and names no addressee. Cell colours were not relied on; column assignment follows the header row and was checked against the page images.

open_questions.question: Does the SS-25-001 attribution requirement (tool name, prompt summary, reviewer identity) apply to every labeled item, including internal and informal content?
open_questions.why_undecided: Section 1.2 says 'Any content generated or assisted by GenAI shall be clearly labeled' and that agencies 'must use standardized attribution formats'. It does not distinguish internal from public content or say who applies the label. GS-25-001 distinguishes informal from 'more official' documents. See C06 and C07.

open_questions.question: How do the meeting provisions fit with the 'Drafting internal summaries' row?
open_questions.why_undecided: GS-25-001 strongly discourages 'AI note-taking tools' in meetings 'held within the State' and tells hosts to keep AI bot note-takers out; SS-25-001 lists 'Use GenAI to summarize meeting notes or internal memos with attribution' as Acceptable. These may address different activities (a bot attending a meeting vs summarizing notes afterwards) but the texts do not say so. 'meetings held within the State' is not explained.

open_questions.question: How do the hiring example and the decision prohibitions fit together?
open_questions.why_undecided: GS-25-001 says 'an HR department may consult with AI platforms in making hiring decisions' but 'may not use AI to scan and reject resumes automatically'. SS-25-001's table says 'Do not use GenAI to make legal, disciplinary, or eligibility decisions' and 'Do not use GenAI to assess employee performance or give personalized advice'. Whether hiring is an 'eligibility' decision, and where consulting ends and deciding begins, is not stated.

open_questions.question: Do the 5 Guiding Principles apply to an individual employee's routine use of a GenAI tool?
open_questions.why_undecided: The principles say they are 'intended to guide state agencies' and 'serve as a framework whenever automated systems have significant implications on the rights of Georgians or their access to essential services'. GS-25-001 says 'all state employees should abide by the 5 Guiding Principles' 'When engaging with generative AI', with no such threshold. Most principles are phrased as agency or system-owner actions. Whether GS-25-001 widens their reach is not decidable from the text.

open_questions.question: Which version of the guiding principles is current?
open_questions.why_undecided: Three texts exist: GS-23-001 (effective 12/12/23), the undated '5 Guiding Principles' web page, and the copy embedded in GS-25-001 (effective 7/1/2025). The last two match in wording; GS-23-001 differs (C11). The web page has no date or identifier.

open_questions.question: Is text missing from GS-25-001 page 9?
open_questions.why_undecided: A lone 'T' follows 'The in-text citation below serves as a good example.' The PDF's text layer and page count are intact and all 12 pages were read; whether a sentence was dropped during drafting cannot be determined from the file.

open_questions.question: Does PS-23-001's passed review date (01/15/2025) affect its status?
open_questions.why_undecided: The copy was captured from the GTA PSG site on 7/21/26, after the review date. No attached document says what a review date means.

open_questions.question: What does 'these requirements' cover in the SS-25-001 enforcement sentence?
open_questions.why_undecided: 'Failure to follow these requirements may result in revocation of tool access and additional oversight actions by GTA' sits at the end of 1.7, before section 2. It could refer to 1.7 only or to all of section 1; it names no party. SS-23-002 section 11 separately provides for discipline of employees, contractors and vendors.

open_questions.question: Does the employee have a personal duty to report incidents or misuse, and to whom?
open_questions.why_undecided: All reporting duties are addressed to agencies (SS-25-001 4.0; SS-23-002 6(d), 8) or are passive (SS-23-002 9(h)). GS-25-001 asks employees to disclose their own AI use on 'the honor system'. No text tells an individual employee whom to notify. See C10 and UR27.

open_questions.question: Does SS-23-002's training requirement apply before an employee may use a GenAI tool, and what training satisfies it?
open_questions.why_undecided: 'All users of AI systems shall undergo appropriate training', including being 'familiarized with this AI Usage Policy'. No training course, timing or record requirement is specified, and 'this AI Usage Policy' is not a title in the corpus (UR28).
